title: Can renewables help forecast prices?
text: Notebook 02 showed that wind and solar lower prices. This notebook asks whether that is useful in practice: if you know how much wind and solar there will be tomorrow, can you forecast tomorrow’s day-ahead prices better?

title: Can renewables help forecast prices?
text:
Key terms

Day-ahead price: the price for each hour of tomorrow, set in an auction the day before. This is what we forecast.
Baseline: a simple rule a model has to beat, such as “tomorrow’s price will equal today’s price at the same hour”.
Training and test data: models learn from 2021–2023 (training) and are graded on 2024–2025 (test), data they have never seen. This mimics forecasting the future.
MAE (mean absolute error): the average size of a forecast’s miss, in $/MWh. Lower is better.
RMSE (root mean squared error): like MAE, but punishes big misses much more. A model with a low MAE but high RMSE is usually right but occasionally very wrong.



Code: load packages and data
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)

ercot <- read_rds(here::here("data/processed/ercot_hourly.rds"))




Code: prepare data
grid <- ercot |>
  filter(hub == "HB_BUSAVG") |>
  arrange(hour_start_utc) |>
  mutate(
    # What is known when tomorrow's forecast is made: today's and last week's
    # day-ahead prices for the same hour.
    price_yesterday = lag(da_price, 24),
    price_last_week = lag(da_price, 168),
    hour_f      = factor(hour_local),
    weekday_f   = factor(as.character(weekday)),
    month_f     = factor(month(time_local)),
    net_load_gw = net_load_mw / 1000,
    uri         = time_local >= as.POSIXct("2021-02-10", tz = "America/Chicago") &
                  time_local <  as.POSIXct("2021-02-21", tz = "America/Chicago")
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(price_last_week), !is.na(net_load_gw))

# Train on 2021-2023 without Winter Storm Uri. Prices are capped at $500 for
# training only, so a handful of extreme hours don't dominate what the models
# learn. Forecasts are always graded against the real, uncapped prices.
train <- grid |>
  filter(year <= 2023, !uri) |>
  mutate(target = pmin(da_price, 500))

test <- filter(grid, year >= 2024)

title: Can renewables help forecast prices?
text:
The forecasts
Four ways to forecast each hour of tomorrow’s day-ahead price:







Forecast
How it works




Same hour yesterday
Tomorrow at 3 p.m. = today at 3 p.m.


Same hour last week
Tomorrow at 3 p.m. = the same weekday last week at 3 p.m.


Time patterns
A regression using recent prices plus hour of day, weekday and month


Time patterns + net load
The same regression, plus tomorrow’s net load



An important caveat: the last model uses the actual net load for each hour. In practice a forecaster would use ERCOT’s published forecasts of demand, wind and solar, which are close but not perfect. So this model shows the best case: how much better forecasts get when net load is known well.


Code: fit the two regression models
m_time <- lm(target ~ price_yesterday + price_last_week + hour_f + weekday_f + month_f,
             data = train)

m_net  <- lm(target ~ price_yesterday + price_last_week + hour_f + weekday_f + month_f +
               net_load_gw + I(net_load_gw^2),
             data = train)

forecasts <- test |>
  mutate(
    `Same hour yesterday`      = price_yesterday,
    `Same hour last week`      = price_last_week,
    `Time patterns`            = predict(m_time, test),
    `Time patterns + net load` = predict(m_net, test)
  )

model_names <- c("Same hour yesterday", "Same hour last week",
                 "Time patterns", "Time patterns + net load")

forecasts_long <- forecasts |>
  select(hour_start_utc, time_local, year, hour_local, da_price, all_of(model_names)) |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(model_names), names_to = "model", values_to = "forecast") |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = model_names),
         error = forecast - da_price)

# Save forecasts for the battery backtest in notebook 04
write_rds(forecasts, here::here("data/processed/forecasts_2024_2025.rds"))

title: Can renewables help forecast prices?
text:
How accurate is each forecast?


Code: forecast errors on 2024–2025
accuracy <- forecasts_long |>
  group_by(model) |>
  summarise(
    mae    = mean(abs(error)),
    rmse   = sqrt(mean(error^2)),
    median = median(abs(error))
  ) |>
  mutate(vs_yesterday = (1 - mae / mae[model == "Same hour yesterday"]) * 100)

knitr::kable(accuracy, digits = 1,
             col.names = c("Forecast", "MAE ($/MWh)", "RMSE ($/MWh)",
                           "Typical miss ($/MWh, median)", "Improvement vs. yesterday (%)"),

Code: chart of forecast errors
ggplot(accuracy, aes(reorder(model, -mae), mae)) +
  geom_col(fill = c("grey60", "grey60", "steelblue", "seagreen")[as.integer(accuracy$model)]) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0("$", round(mae, 1))), vjust = -0.4) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Average miss (MAE, $/MWh)",
       title = "Average forecast error on 2024–2025")









Findings: Electricity prices are hard to predict. The simplest guess, “same price as yesterday”, was the most accurate, missing by about $13/MWh on average. Our regression models did not beat it.
Still, adding wind, solar and demand to the model made its forecasts better. This supports what notebook 02 found: wind and solar affect prices, so knowing how much there will be helps predict them. A better model would be needed to turn that into forecasts that beat the simple guess.

title: Can renewables help forecast prices?
text:
What the forecasts look like
One summer week in 2024. The black line is the actual day-ahead price.


Code: forecasts vs. actual for one week
week_start <- as.POSIXct("2024-08-18", tz = "America/Chicago")

forecasts_long |>
  filter(time_local >= week_start, time_local < week_start + days(7),
         model %in% c("Same hour yesterday", "Time patterns + net load")) |>
  ggplot(aes(time_local)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = da_price, colour = "Actual price"), linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = forecast, colour = "Forecast"), linewidth = 1.1,
            linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~ model, ncol = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Actual price" = "black", "Forecast" = "#E66100")) +
  scale_x_datetime(date_breaks = "1 day", date_labels = "%a %b %d") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Day-ahead price ($/MWh)", colour = NULL,
       title = "Forecasts vs. actual prices, Aug 18–24, 2024") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())









Findings: The top panel shows the “same as yesterday” forecast. It follows normal hours closely, but it is always one day late on spikes: after the $635 spike on August 20, it predicted another one on August 21, when the price only reached about $120.
The bottom panel shows the regression model. It correctly expects prices to rise every evening, but it misjudges how much: it underestimated the biggest spikes (about $290 instead of $635) and guessed too high on calmer days later in the week.

title: Can renewables help forecast prices?
section: Where do the forecasts miss most?
text:
Where do the forecasts miss most?


Code: average miss by hour of day
forecasts_long |>
  group_by(model, hour_local) |>
  summarise(mae = mean(abs(error)), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(hour_local, mae, colour = model)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey60", "grey80", "steelblue", "seagreen")) +
  labs(x = "Hour of day (Central)", y = "Average miss (MAE, $/MWh)", colour = NULL,
       title = "Forecast errors by hour of day")











Code: average miss on normal vs. expensive hours
forecasts_long |>
  mutate(price_level = if_else(da_price > 100, "Expensive hours (above $100)",
                               "Normal hours ($100 or less)")) |>
  group_by(price_level, model) |>
  summarise(hours = n(), mae = mean(abs(error)), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = price_level, values_from = c(hours, mae)) |>
  select(model, starts_with("mae")) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1,
               col.names = c("Forecast", "MAE: expensive hours", "MAE: normal hours"),
               caption = "Average miss ($/MWh) on normal vs. expensive hours")

Findings: All forecasts miss most around 7 p.m., when solar fades and prices jump, and least overnight and at midday, when prices are steady.
Which forecast is best depends on the hour. On normal hours, “same as yesterday” is the most accurate, off by about $10/MWh. On expensive hours (above $100/MWh), the model with net load is the most accurate, off by about $119/MWh compared with $172 for “same as yesterday”. Net load helps most in the afternoon, when solar is strongest: knowing how much solar there will be lets the model predict those hours much better.

title: Can renewables help forecast prices?
text:
Takeaway
Findings: No single forecast was best everywhere. A simple rule (“same price as yesterday”) worked best on ordinary hours, while the model with net load worked best on the expensive hours that matter most. This supports notebook 02: knowing how much wind and solar there will be helps predict the hours when power is most expensive.

Sanity checks

Solar output should peak around 1 p.m. Central. A peak at noon or 2 p.m. would mean the hour conversion is off by one.

What does an average day look like?
Summer is June–August and winter is December–February. Price uses the median, so a few extreme hours (like Winter Storm Uri) don’t distort the daily shape.


Code: average day by season
daily <- grid |>
  mutate(season = case_when(
    month(time_local) %in% 6:8       ~ "Summer",
    month(time_local) %in% c(12, 1, 2) ~ "Winter"
  )) |>
  filter(!is.na(season)) |>
  group_by(season, hour_local) |>
  summarise(
    `Demand (MW)`       = mean(demand_mw, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Wind (MW)`         = mean(wind_mw, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Solar (MW)`        = mean(solar_mw, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Net load (MW)`     = mean(net_load_mw, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Median RT price ($/MWh)` = median(rt_price),
    .groups = "drop"

       title = "An average day on the ERCOT grid, summer vs. winter")

Code: West hub discount vs. wind output
west_vs_wind <- ercot |>
  filter(hub %in% c("HB_WEST", "HB_BUSAVG")) |>
  select(hour_start_utc, hub, rt_price, wind_mw) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = hub, values_from = rt_price) |>
  mutate(wind_bin = cut(wind_mw, breaks = seq(0, 30000, 5000),
                        labels = c("0–5k", "5–10k", "10–15k", "15–20k", "20–25k", "25–30k"))) |>
  filter(!is.na(wind_bin)) |>
  group_by(wind_bin) |>
  summarise(west_minus_system = median(HB_WEST - HB_BUSAVG), hours = n())

ggplot(west_vs_wind, aes(wind_bin, west_minus_system)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey40") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("$%.2f", west_minus_system)),
            vjust = ifelse(west_vs_wind$west_minus_system < 0, 1.5, -0.5)) +
  geom_text(aes(y = 1.5, label = paste(scales::comma(hours), "hours")),
            size = 3, colour = "grey30") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(min(west_vs_wind$west_minus_system) - 1.5, 2.5)) +
  labs(x = "ERCOT wind output (MW)",
       y = "West price minus statewide price ($/MWh, median)",
       title = "West Texas power gets cheaper only on very windy hours",
       subtitle = "Below 20,000 MW of wind, West and the rest of Texas pay about the same")









Findings: The West hub is priced the same as the rest of Texas until wind output passes about 20,000 MW. Above that, West is about $6/MWh cheaper, and about $10 cheaper above 25,000 MW. Most Texas wind farms are in West Texas, and on very windy hours the power lines carrying that power east fill up, so the extra power is stuck in the West and its price drops.

title: ERCOT Power Prices and Renewables
text:
Wind and solar lower Texas power prices, most of all when the grid is under strain.

Renewables are growing fast. From 2021 to 2025, average solar output grew more than fourfold, passing nuclear and coal; wind grew about 20%.
They lower prices. Each 10-point increase in wind and solar’s share of demand cuts the real-time price by about $12/MWh ($9.50 day-ahead), comparing only similar hours and excluding Winter Storm Uri.
The effect is biggest when the grid is tight. In summer the drop is about $23/MWh, twice the winter effect. Prices stay low until the demand left for gas, coal and nuclear plants passes about 60,000 MW, then climb sharply, reaching a typical $488/MWh in the rarest, tightest hours.
Prices peak in the evening, not when demand is highest. As solar fades after sunset, other plants must fill the gap, so summer prices peak around 8 p.m., three hours after peak demand.
Location matters. West Texas, home to most wind farms, sees the largest drop ($16/MWh). On very windy hours, power lines to the rest of the state fill up and West prices fall up to $10 below the statewide price.
The effect tracks gas prices. It was largest in 2022, when natural gas was expensive, and by 2025 renewables explained more than twice as much of the hour-to-hour price swings as in earlier years.

title: ERCOT Power Prices and Renewables
text:
The analysis

Exploring the data: data checks, how the grid has changed, and what drives prices through the day.
Do wind and solar lower prices?: how much prices fall as renewables grow, by year, season and region.
Forecasting prices: whether knowing net load (demand minus wind and solar) makes day-ahead price forecasts better.

Coming next: whether a battery using these findings would have made money.

title: ERCOT Power Prices and Renewables
text:
Data
Hourly real-time and day-ahead prices at ERCOT’s trading hubs (ERCOT), and hourly demand and generation by fuel (U.S. Energy Information Administration, EIA-930). Both are public and free; the data is not stored in the repository, but the README explains how to download it and rebuild every result.

title: Do wind and solar lower prices?
text:
The main question of the project: when more of demand is met by wind and solar, how much lower is the price, and does that effect change over time?
Code: load packages and data
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)

# Run the scripts in R/ first (see the README).
ercot <- read_rds(here::here("data/processed/ercot_hourly.rds"))
Code: prepare modeling data
base <- ercot |>
  filter(hub == "HB_BUSAVG", !is.na(renewable_share)) |>
  mutate(
    hour_f  = factor(hour_local),
    month_f = factor(month(time_local)),
    year_f  = factor(year),
    uri     = time_local >= as.POSIXct("2021-02-10", tz = "America/Chicago") &
              time_local <  as.POSIXct("2021-02-21", tz = "America/Chicago"),
    season  = case_when(month(time_local) %in% 6:8        ~ "Summer",
                        month(time_local) %in% c(12, 1, 2) ~ "Winter",
                        TRUE                               ~ "Spring/Fall")
  )

no_uri <- filter(base, !uri)

# Effect of renewables on price, per 10 percentage points of renewable share
effect <- function(model) {
  tibble(
    effect_per_10pp = coef(model)[["renewable_share"]] * 0.1,
    std_error       = sqrt(diag(vcov(model)))[["renewable_share"]] * 0.1,
    r_squared       = summary(model)$r.squared,
    hours           = nobs(model)
  )
}

title: Do wind and solar lower prices?
Do wind and solar lower prices?
text:
Model

How much do renewables lower prices?
Each model adds one thing:

Renewable share alone.
Adds hour, month and year, so the comparison is between hours that are otherwise alike (same time of day, same season, same year).
Model 2 without Winter Storm Uri.
Model 3 using day-ahead instead of real-time prices.



Code: regression models
models <- list(
  "1. Renewable share only"             = lm(rt_price ~ renewable_share, base),
  "2. + hour, month, year controls"     = lm(rt_price ~ renewable_share + hour_f + month_f + year_f, base),
  "3. Model 2 without Winter Storm Uri" = lm(rt_price ~ renewable_share + hour_f + month_f + year_f, no_uri),
  "4. Model 3 with day-ahead price"     = lm(da_price ~ renewable_share + hour_f + month_f + year_f, no_uri)
)

map_dfr(models, effect, .id = "model") |>
  knitr::kable(digits = c(0, 2, 2, 3, 0),
               caption = "Change in price ($/MWh) for each 10-point rise in renewable share")

Findings: More wind and solar means lower prices. After comparing only similar hours (same time of day, month and year) and removing Winter Storm Uri, each 10-point increase in wind and solar’s share of demand lowers the real-time price by about $12/MWh, and the day-ahead price by about $9.50/MWh.
Including Uri more than triples the estimate (to about $42), because that one week combined very little wind and solar with $9,000 prices. We use the estimate without Uri, since a single extreme event shouldn’t drive the result.
Renewable share explains only 6–10% of the hour-to-hour swings in price; most of the variation comes from rare price spikes that depend on other things, such as demand and power plant outages.


Has the effect changed over time?


Code: effect by year
by_year <- no_uri |>
  group_by(year) |>
  group_modify(~ effect(lm(rt_price ~ renewable_share + hour_f + month_f, data = .x))) |>
  ungroup()

ggplot(by_year, aes(factor(year), effect_per_10pp)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey40") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = effect_per_10pp - 1.96 * std_error,
                    ymax = effect_per_10pp + 1.96 * std_error), width = 0.2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0("$", round(effect_per_10pp, 1))),
            vjust = ifelse(by_year$effect_per_10pp < 0, 1.8, -0.8), colour = "white") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Price change per 10-point rise in renewable share ($/MWh)",
       title = "Effect of renewables on price, by year")

Findings: Renewables lowered prices in every year, by about $10–13/MWh per 10-point increase, except in 2022, when the effect nearly doubled to about $20. 2022 was a year of expensive natural gas, so every MWh of wind and solar replaced costlier gas power and saved more. As gas got cheaper in 2023–2024, the effect shrank back.
In 2025, renewables explain far more of the hour-to-hour price swings (23%, up from 7–10% in earlier years). As solar has grown, it has become a bigger driver of when power is cheap or expensive.

Findings: Renewables lower prices most in summer, about $23/MWh per 10-point increase, twice as much as in winter ($10) or spring and fall ($12). Summer is when the grid is tightest, so extra wind and solar keep expensive peaker plants switched off.
West Texas sees the biggest drop ($16/MWh), compared with $11–12 at the other hubs. Most wind farms are in West Texas, and when power lines to the rest of the state fill up, the extra power stays local and pushes West prices down further. Houston, farthest from the wind farms, sees the smallest effect ($11).
A note on uncertainty: the uncertainty numbers in these tables assume each hour is independent, but neighboring hours are very similar (same weather, same power plants running). That makes the true uncertainty larger than shown. The conclusions don’t change: the effects are far enough from zero that renewables clearly lower prices, but the exact dollar amounts should be read as estimates.

title: Do wind and solar lower prices?
text:
Takeaway
Wind and solar lower Texas power prices, most of all when the grid is under strain.

Renewables are growing fast. From 2021 to 2025, average solar output grew more than fourfold, passing nuclear and coal; wind grew about 20%.
They lower prices. Each 10-point increase in wind and solar’s share of demand cuts the real-time price by about $12/MWh ($9.50 day-ahead), comparing only similar hours and excluding Winter Storm Uri.
The effect is biggest when the grid is tight. In summer the drop is about $23/MWh, twice the winter effect. Prices stay low until the demand left for gas, coal and nuclear plants passes about 60,000 MW, then climb sharply, reaching a typical $488/MWh in the rarest, tightest hours.
Prices peak in the evening, not when demand is highest. As solar fades after sunset, other plants must fill the gap, so summer prices peak around 8 p.m., three hours after peak demand.
Location matters. West Texas, home to most wind farms, sees the largest drop ($16/MWh). On very windy hours, power lines to the rest of the state fill up and West prices fall up to $10 below the statewide price.
The effect tracks gas prices. It was largest in 2022, when natural gas was expensive, and by 2025 renewables explained more than twice as much of the hour-to-hour price swings as in earlier years.
